thread.title: 6 Reasons I'm Skipping The Xiaomi IPO - Xiaomi (BATS:XI)

author: Tariq Dennison
title: 6 Reasons I'm Skipping The Xiaomi IPO - Xiaomi (BATS:XI)
text:
Xiaomi ( XI ) is a Chinese technology company primarily known for making high-quality, low-cost smartphones that outsell Apple Inc.'s ( AAPL ) iPhone in China. The company recently announced an IPO shortly after the Hong Kong exchange made a change to the HKEX listing rules to allow for dual share classes. Because these rule changes were clearly understood to be in response to Alibaba Group Holding Limited's ( BABA ) decision to list in New York instead of Hong Kong four years ago, and Hong Kong's desire to not miss another hot tech IPO, the Xiaomi IPO has been loosely compared to Alibaba's. Both are large and fast-growing Chinese technology companies with the internationally listed shares holding a complex Cayman company structure, but Xiaomi faces greater headwinds to investors seeking a repeat of Alibaba's returns.
Although I usually avoid most IPOs anyway, especially hot ones, I have been asked enough about this one, I felt it was worth listing below six main reasons I decided to skip the Xiaomi IPO.
Lei Jun and his co-founders started Xiaomi in April 2010 initially to "create a very cool smartphone that we would personally love", according to the open letter from the chairman on page 1 of the global offering document on the HKEX website. I first discovered the company in late 2013 at a bitcoin event when an attendee pulled out a smartphone with what seemed like a high-quality screen and camera that he said he ordered online for only about HK$1,000 (US$130) from this company called Xiaomi (which means "little rice" in Chinese). As clear from the screenshot below of the Hong Kong site, Xiaomi has expanded both into much higher-end smartphones costing half as much as an iPhone X to wearables competing with Fitbit, Inc. ( FIT ) and even electric toothbrushes competing with Philips's Sonicare. They also make some of the best portable battery phone charger power banks I have used, which makes sense given the number of their products that rely on batteries.
Source: mi.com/hk
#1: The Xiaomi IPO is still "too hot" I consider myself a value-oriented and somewhat contrarian investor, so naturally tend to avoid investing in anything I feel too many investors with more money and information than me are paying attention to. The BABA IPO in 2014 scared me away because too many institutional investors "had to" buy it because it was so big and they could not miss out. Yes, that means I missed out on the opportunity to more than double my money in less than four years, but I make money by buying streams of annual dollar bills for $10, not by buying a growing stream of pennies that are now selling for $20 that I hope someone will pay me $40 for soon enough.
Over the past few days, I was in Shanghai and saw ads for Xiaomi 6 and 2S phones with young, attractive models posted all over town and still saw them on trams when I got back to Hong Kong. Below is an example of an ad from the Mi.com website very similar to the 10' high ones I've seen plastered inside the metro stations across Hong Kong and Shanghai this week.
Source: Mi.com
That amount of publicity means I'd probably be competing with too much excitement over the IPO to get an attractive enough valuation, which brings me to...
#2: As with too many tech IPOs that get this much attention, the valuation is sky high On page 23, the offering document estimates a market cap of HK$380-492 billion (US$50-70 billion) based on the offer price range of HK$17-22/share. That is about 3-4x Xiaomi's 2017 top-line revenue of RMB115 billion (US$17 billion), which prices in extremely optimistic expectations in my view, especially given the margins mentioned below. In this, I don't seem to be alone, as other institutional investors have also addressed concerns over valuation.
#3: The business faces too much competition While proponents might want to compare Xiaomi to Alibaba or Apple, Xiaomi faces far greater competition and narrower moats from any network effects. Case in point, I recently found myself shopping for a high-end Android phone to compliment my old iPhone and didn't want to pay up for the top Samsung or Huawei, so narrowed down to one of the Xiaomi's or a OnePlus 6. I owned a Xiaomi back in 2014, and mostly liked it, but disliked the software they put on top of Android enough to not buy another one when I lost that phone in a Chinese taxi. When I test drove the Xiaomi 2S at a pop-up show in Hong Kong, I found enough of the user interface that I didn't like in the old Xiaomi seemed to remain the same, so I chose the OnePlus 6 for the cleaner software and user interface. I have found a far harder time switching between the iPhone and any Android phone than I do switching between any two Android phones (of which my last Android phone was a Lenovo Vibe shot, which I gave to my 10-year old), and so even in my own experience, Xiaomi does not seem to have enough of an ecosystem lock-in or switching costs like Apple to create any kind of moat around its software business. Xiaomi brags that it caps the profit margins on its hardware business at 5% so that it can focus on getting more users into its higher margin software ecosystem, but while most people in China have trouble living without Tencent Holding Ltd.'s ( OTCPK:TCEHY ) WeChat or Alibaba's Taobao (the Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN ) of China), I haven't met anyone in all my time in China who has shown me a Xiaomi app they can't live without. Competition is one of the 7 C's I listed that would probably crush Tesla .
#4: The ownership and control structure is too complicated Even though I am quite used to the complex ownership and insider-friendly control structures of many Asian-listed companies, this one clearly would not make my top 10 list of stocks I would expect my 10-year old to understand anytime soon. More likely, I would use this offering document as a timely example for Masters in Finance students on a company that not only went from almost zero (US$50,000 in initial capital) to $70 billion in just over 7 years but also of the many complexities common in offshore-listed Chinese companies. Even then, I probably wouldn't be too hard on Masters students who had trouble understanding parts of this investment after only one semester.
Xiaomi's Hong Kong-listed shares (01810.HK) and US BATS traded XI would be considered "P-chips", being listed shares of a company incorporated in the Cayman Islands, but whose business is mostly in Mainland China and run by a private sector Chinese entrepreneur. This is a different distinction than the difference between A shares, H shares, and N shares I described in this earlier reference article in that the "P" in P chips describe who runs the company (a private entrepreneur, rather than a government entity like in a Red chip) as well as the fact that it is incorporated in a Caribbean tax haven.
The below excerpt from page 15 of the offering document also summarises the Variable Interest Entity (VIE) structure. In this VIE, the Hong Kong-listed, Cayman incorporated Xiaomi corporation owns a Wholly Foreign Owned Enterprise (WFOE) in Mainland China. Because of restrictions, the WFOE does not directly own the Xiaomi-branded smartphone or software businesses operating in Mainland China, but rather has a contract to provide services in exchange for "service fees" that effectively provide offshore shareholders (through the WFOE) a proportional share of the onshore businesses' profits. Last year, the Economist brilliantly described VIE's as the "Too Big to Fail" of Chinese stocks listed outside China.
Source: Offering Document
As I am surrounded by them and continue to see opportunity to find value and make money in them, I don't immediately dismiss investing in a VIE, I am just a little more cautious about them, especially at the IPO phase before overseas markets have had the chance to see a few annual reports (and preferably a dividend or buyback).
#5: The path to big future profits is also too complicated and uncertain The high valuation seems to imply that Xiaomi will easily be able to shift its business from the highly competitive low-margin hardware business to being a high-margin, high-moat ecosystem like that of Apple and its iCloud services. This would solve reason #3, but actually doing this will be far harder than Apple made it look, especially with the ecosystems already established by Alibaba and Tencent that would leave it too easy to switch from a Xiaomi to a Samsung or OnePlus.
While I would like to be optimistic about the potential for Xiaomi to become one of the best integrated brands in the IoT and smart home space (for example, getting your Xiaomi fitness band, air filter, electric toothbrush, and a dozen other appliances to all talk to each other and your doctor through Xiaomi apps), there are way too many variables and things that could go wrong to justify the offered valuation.
#6: The IPO is clearly aimed at retail investors who would never be able to read and understand the prospectus in time Perhaps my biggest mission in the world of investing is to help every day savers better understand how the stocks in their retirement plans make money. As hinted in #4, I would not expect most of the individuals considering subscribing to the Xiaomi IPO because they are as fascinated by their phones and growth story to be able to digest and process the 697-page offering document in the 78 hours between when the offering documents were made public on the HKEX website and when the subscription forms are due. Even though I enjoy reading offering documents and evaluate investments for a living, I would find this to be a challenge, and can't imagine how an average investor would be expected to make an informed decision so quickly.
Global offering documents were posted on the official HKEXNews.hk website around 6 AM HK time on June 25th...
... but the IPO subscription forms were due at noon Hong Kong time on June 28th, from page i of the 697 page offering document .
Conclusion I would be one of the first to admit that I am extremely impressed with Xiaomi's products and how it built such an amazing business and brand in such a short time to compete with the likes of Apple, but I also avoid confusing a good product or a good story with a good stock. While Xiaomi has a good chance to continue its phenomenal growth and double IPO investors money as quickly as Alibaba has done, Xiaomi lacks many of the unique advantages and network effects that would protect this path the way customers are locked in to Alibaba or Tencent's services. At this point, I think buying the Xiaomi IPO is too much a bet on a highly optimistic expectation of future growth and an IoT vision, and not enough of a value relative to high-probability fundamentals, so I am avoiding it for now.
Disclosure: I/we have no positions in any stocks mentioned, and no plans to initiate any positions within the next 72 hours.
